INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
Michigan Coalition for Responsible Gun Owners
(“MCRGO”) is a Michigan non-partisan, nonprofit
corporation, founded in 1996 to support and defend
the right to keep and bear arms through education,
legislation, and litigation. MCRGO has thousands of
members statewide, with members residing in every
Michigan county. MCRGO has a particular interest in
the historical and doctrinal principles governing the
Second and Fourteenth Amendments and in ensuring
that modern firearms restrictions are assessed under
the historical method this Court has prescribed.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The Second Amendment recognizes a pre -existing
right of the people and commands that it “shall not be
infringed.” District of Columbia v. Heller , 554 U.S.
570, 592 (2008). Once the Amendment’s text covers
the conduct at issue, the government must establish
that its restriction is consistent with the Nation’s
historical tradition of firearm regulation. The lower
courts inverted that inquiry by trea ting a
semiautomatic rifle’s military ancestry, asserted
effectiveness, or resemblance to military equipment
as a reason to remove it from the people’s right.
United States v. Miller , 307 U.S. 174 (1939), as
interpreted by Heller, points the other way. The
founding-era militia consisted of citizens who
privately possessed lawful arms and ordinarily

1 Pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 37.6, no counsel for a party

2
brought those arms to service. That history may not
establish a right to every weapon used by a modern
armed force, but it forecloses treating military
relevance itself as a categorical reason to deny
protection. The government must instead identify a
distinct, well -established historical principle
supporting a comparable modern burden.
Reconstruction reinforces that discipline but does
not transform this arm-based case into a status-based
one. Antebellum and Black Code restrictions often
rested on judgments about the status of the persons
burdened. The Fourteenth Amendment and the
Freedmen’s Bureau Act repudiated that status order.
Such status -based restrictions do not establish a
tradition of prohibiting an entire class of bearable
arms from possession by the people generally.
The same principle governs the phrase “dangerous
and unusual.” That historically defined, conjunctive
limitation does not permit courts to exclude arms
based on lethality, military lineage, or asserted
effectiveness. Bruen, Rahimi, and Wolford require a
relevantly similar historical analogue imposing a
comparable burden for a comparable reason.
Restrictions directed at threatening conduct,
individualized dangerousness, or a historically
recognized status may supply rules in their proper
settings. None establishes that a semiautomatic rifle
becomes unprotected because it resembles military
equipment or is thought particularly effective.
The courts below relied materially on that broader
inference, while the Third Circuit reached the
contrary result in Ass’n of N.J. Rifle & Pistol Clubs,
Inc. v. Att’y Gen. N.J., 183 F.4th 211 (3d Cir. 2026). It
held that New Jersey had not demonstrated a
sufficiently analogous historical tradition to justify a
prohibition on semiautomatic rifles. This Court

3
should reject military association and generalized
dangerousness as substitutes for the historically
grounded principle the Second Amendment inquiry
requires.
ARGUMENT
I. THE SECOND AMENDMENT RECOGNIZES
A PRE-EXISTING RIGHT AND LIMITS
GOVERNMENTAL POWER; THE FOUNDING-
ERA MILITIA SYSTEM CONFIRMS, RATHER
THAN DEFEATS, THAT LIMITATION.
The Second Amendment does not grant the people
a right created by the Constitution. It recognizes a
pre-existing right and commands that it “shall not be
infringed.” Heller, 554 U.S. at 592. History therefore
identifies the historically understood limits on
governmental power over that right; it does not
authorize government to revise the right’s scope based
upon contemporary judgments about a firearm’s
military utility, let hality, or asserted necessity for
ordinary self-defense.
A. The English settlement limited prerogative
disarmament but retained a status-bound
right.
The English antecedents of the Second
Amendment arose from seventeenth-century disputes
concerning royal prerogative, standing forces, militia
authority, and selective possession of arms. The
Petition of Right objected to forced quartering and
martial law in peacetime, and control of the militia
became central to the constitutional conflict preceding
the English Civil War. See Petition of Right, 3 Car. 1,
c. 1 (1628); Lois G. Schwoerer, The Declaration of
Rights, 1689 42–69 (1981).

4
The grievances against James II joined those
concerns. The Declaration of Rights charged the
Crown with maintaining a standing army in
peacetime without parliamentary consent and with
causing Protestant subjects to be disarmed while
Catholics were armed an d employed contrary to law.
Bill of Rights 1689, 1 W. & M., sess. 2, c. 2. The
ensuing arms guarantee was meaningful but
qualified: Protestant subjects could possess arms for
defense if suitable to their conditions and allowed by
law. Blackstone later described the right as auxiliary
to self -preservation while retaining those
qualifications. 1 William Blackstone, Commentaries
on the Laws of England *139–40.
The English experience therefore supplied both an
inheritance and a limitation. It associated selective
executive disarmament with constitutional abuse, but
it did not remove the right’s scope from a system
organized around subjecthood, legal status, and
parliamentary supremacy. The American Revolution
inherited the constitutional problem while rejecting
the authority structure within which the English
settlement had operated.
B. The Founding combined governmental
military power with an armed citizenry.
The Constitution substantially enlarged federal
military authority. Congress could raise armies,
maintain a navy, call forth the militia, and provide for
organizing, arming, and disciplining it. U.S. Const.
art. I, § 8. But the ratification -era defense of those
powers did not posit a citizenry  constitutionally
external to armed defense. Madison referred to “the
advantage of being armed, which the Americans
possess over the people of almost every other nation,”
and contemplated citizens with arms in their hands

5
organized under lawful authority. The Federalist No.
46, at 299 (James Madison) (Jacob E. Cooke ed., 1961).
The state constitutional and ratification materials
reflect the same arrangement. Virginia described a
militia “composed of the body of the people, trained to
arms” as the proper defense of a free State. Va.
Declaration of Rights § 13 (1776). Pennsylvania
recognized the people’s right to bear arms for defense
of themselves and the State. Pa. Declaration of Rights
§§ 13 –14 (1776). New Hampshire proposed that
Congress should never disarm a citizen except one in
actual rebellion. 1 Jonathan Elliot, The Debates in the
Several State Conventions on the Adoption of the
Federal Constitution 326–27 (2d ed. 1836).
The Second Amendment constitutionalized that
relationship in a single provision: a well -regulated
militia is necessary to the security of a free State,
while the right of the people to keep and bear arms
shall not be infringed. U.S. Const. amend. II. Heller
holds that the operative clause protects an individual
right rather than a right confined to formal militia
service. 554 U.S. at 577 –600. The Militia Act of 1792
likewise required enrolled citizens to provide
themselves with specified arms and equipment. Act of
May 8, 1792, ch. 33, § 1, 1 Stat. 271, 271.
The Constitution and early militia laws therefore
did not presume a divide between privately held arms
and arms relevant to collective defense. To  the
contrary, they proceeded from the premise that the
militia consisted of citizens who retained arms in
private life and would appear for public service with
those arms. The constitutional concern was not that
citizens might possess arms useful in organ ized
defense; it was that a government possessing military
power might disarm the people from whom the militia
was drawn. Under the heading “The Right is General,”

6
Cooley later rejected the notion that the militia clause
confined the right to formally enrolled members:
It may be supposed from the phraseology of this
provision that the right to keep and bear arms
was only guaranteed to the militia; but this
would be an interpretation not warranted by
the intent. The militia, as has been elsewhere
explained, consists of those persons who, under
the law, are liable to the performance of
military duty, and are officered and enrolled for
service when called upon. . . . [I]f the right were
limited to those enrolled, the purpose of this
guaranty might be defeated altogether by the
action or neglect to act of the government it was
meant to hold in check. The meaning of the
provision undoubtedly is, that the people, from
whom the militia must be taken, shall have the
right to keep and bear arms, and they need no
permission or regulation of law for the purpose.
Thomas M. Cooley, The General Principles of
Constitutional Law in the United States of
America 298 (3d ed. 1898).
United States v. Miller , 307 U.S. 174 (1939),
confirms that historical reference point. Although the
Court rejected the particular challenge before it
because the record did not show that the short -
barreled shotgun bore the required relationship to a
well-regulated militia,  id. at  178, its account of the
militia is clear. The militia consisted of citizens
capable of acting together for the common defense,
who ordinarily appeared for service with arms they
had supplied themselves and that were “of the kind in
common use at the time.” Id. at 179.
District of Columbia v. Heller  supplies the
controlling interpretation of Miller. Heller explained
that the traditional militia was drawn from citizens

7
who brought to militia duty the lawful weapons they
possessed at home. 554 U.S. 570, 624, 627 (2008). That
is precisely the way the operative clause’s individual
right furthered the militia purpose. Id. at 627. Miller,
as interpreted by Heller, therefore confirms that the
Second Amendment’s historical reference point was a
citizen militia carrying privately possessed lawful
arms.
That principle does not establish a right to every
weapon used by a modern armed force. Heller
recognizes that M-16 rifles and similar weapons may
be prohibited. Id. But it forecloses the inverse
proposition advanced by respondents and adopted by
the courts below: that military utility, military
lineage, or resemblance to modern military equipment
is itself a categorical exclusion from the right. The
historical relat ionship was overlapping rather than
mutually exclusive. A government seeking to prohibit
a class of otherwise bearable arms must identify the
separate historical principle that authorizes that
prohibition. The historical examples in the next
section reinforce this important distinction. They
show why a historical restriction directed at
particular persons or conduct cannot be severed from
its burden and justification and converted into a
categorical rule about a class of arms.
II. RECONSTRUCTION-ERA STATUS-BASED
DISARMAMENT LAWS DO NOT ESTABLISH A
HISTORICAL TRADITION OF PROHIBITING
CLASSES OF ARMS.
The Fourteenth Amendment repudiates status -
based disarmament. Historical regulations must
therefore be understood in their actual legal context
and cannot be stripped of their limiting principle to
create a generalized governmental power over arms.

8
The dispute over whether 1791 or 1868 supplies the
principal historical reference point does not displace
that constitutional command. To the extent
Reconstruction-era evidence informs a Second
Amendment case, a court may not treat every state
firearms res triction enacted near Reconstruction as
neutral evidence of the right’s scope. The Fourteenth
Amendment was adopted to displace the legal order
that enforced subordinate civic status, not to preserve
that order as a source of regulatory authority over
citizens generally.
Before Reconstruction, arms disabilities did not
rest on a single principle. States regulated
threatening conduct, concealed carry, and dangerous
misuse. But other disabilities followed an antecedent
judgment that particular persons stood outside equal
civic membership. State v. Newsom, 27 N.C. (5 Ired.)
250 (1844), illustrates the distinction. The court
sustained North Carolina’s firearms restriction on
free persons of color because they were not regarded
as citizens “in the largest sense of the term.” Id. at
254–55. The disability thus reflected a legal status
judgment, not a generally applicable conclusion that
the arms at issue were categorically unfit for citizens.
Dred Scott v. Sandford, 60 U.S. (19 How.) 393 (1857),
made the inverse connection: it identified the ability
to keep and carry arms as one consequence of
citizenship precisely while denying Black persons that
status. Id. at 417.
After emancipation, Southern Black Codes
attempted to preserve forms of subordinate civic
status, including through restrictions on firearms
possession. Congress responded in the language of
equal citizenship, personal security, and
constitutional right. S ection 14 of the Freedmen’s
Bureau Act of 1866 secured, without respect to race or

9
previous condition of slavery, the full and equal
benefit of laws concerning personal liberty and
personal security, including “the constitutional right
to bear arms.” Act of July 16, 1866, ch. 200, § 14, 14
Stat. 173, 176 –77. And the Fourteenth Amendment
altered the constitutional relationship between
citizens and state governments. McDonald v. City of
Chicago, 561 U.S. 742, 770 –78 (2010) (plurality
opinion).
The point is not that all Reconstruction -era
firearm regulations are irrelevant, nor that
respondents rely on Black Codes. It is narrower. The
Fourteenth Amendment cannot be understood by
treating the very disabilities it repudiated as neutral
evidence of a general power to disarm citizens. A
historical restriction cannot be abstracted from its
legal object, target, mechanism, and justification,
then converted into a generalized governmental
authority over arms.
That principle applies beyond status-based laws. A
restriction directed at a subordinated class,
threatening conduct, a judicially identified dangerous
person, gunpowder storage, a particular manner of
carry, or automatic -fire weapons has a defined
historical object and burden. It may illuminate the
historically understood limits of the right in its own
setting. But it does not establish that government may
categorically prohibit law -abiding citizens from
possessing a class of semiautomatic rifles merely
because the modern restriction and the historical law
both concern weapons or public safety.
Reconstruction therefore supplies the necessary
rule of historical classification. Historical regulations
must be read according to the persons burdened, the
conduct regulated, the mechanism imposed, and the

10
purpose served. The modern cases require precisely
that discipline.
The question, then, is not whether history contains
weapons regulations. It is whether respondents have
identified a historical limitation on the people’s right
that is genuinely comparable in target, mechanism,
burden, and justification to the categorical  rifle
restrictions at issue. Bruen, Rahimi, and Wolford
require that showing.
III. THE GOVERNMENT MUST
DEMONSTRATE A HISTORICALLY
GROUNDED LIMITATION ON THE PEOPLE’S
RIGHT; MILITARY RESEMBLANCE AND
GENERALIZED DANGEROUSNESS DO NOT
SATISFY THAT BURDEN.
A. Bruen, Rahimi, and Wolford place the
burden on government.
Once the Second Amendment’s text covers the
conduct at issue, the Constitution presumptively
protects that conduct. N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n
v. Bruen requires the government to demonstrate that
its restriction is consistent with the Nation’s historical
tradition of firearm regulation. 597 U.S. 1, 24 (2022).
The premise is crucial: history identifies the limits on
governmental power over a pre -existing right; it does
not give government a free -ranging authority to
redefine that right based on present-day assessments
of a weapon’s utility or danger. Historical analogies
need not be identical, but the inquiry asks whether
modern and historical regulations impose comparable
burdens for comparable reasons —their “how” and
“why.” Id. at 29–30. The government must identify a
well-established and representative analogue, not an
isolated law or a superficial resemblance. Id. at 30.

11
United States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S. 680 (2024),
confirms that analogical reasoning is neither a
regulatory straightjacket nor a blank check. Its
holding concerned a targeted disarmament restriction
applicable after a court found that the covered person
posed a credible threat to an intimate partner or child.
Id. at 698 –700. The object, trigger, burden, and
justification of that person -specific restriction differ
from a categorical ban on a class of semiautomatic
rifles possessed by citizens generally. Rahimi thus
supplies no rule that a historically supported
restriction on dangerous persons automatically
validates a restriction on an arm category.
Wolford v. Lopez, 609 U.S. ___ (2026), applies the
required discipline directly. Hawaii relied in part on
an 1865 Louisiana enactment that barred carrying
firearms on another person’s “premises or
plantations” without consent. 1865 La. Acts No. 10, §
1, at 14. This Court declined to give that law weight
because it was neither widespread nor widely
accepted. It also explained that the enactment
belonged to Louisiana’s Black Code and was designed
to subordinate and disarm newly freed Black
persons—a purpose materially differ ent from
Hawaii’s modern justification. Wolford, slip op. at 23–
24.
Wolford does not render every discriminatory or
Reconstruction-era law categorically irrelevant. Nor is
it an analogue concerning a ban on semiautomatic
rifles. Its lesson is methodological: the fact that two
laws concern firearms does not establish similarity. A
proffered historical law must be evaluated in its
actual constitutional setting —who was burdened,
what conduct was restricted, how the restriction
operated, and why it was imposed.

12
That method governs respondents’ reliance on
military association. The question is not whether the
relevant rifles have some connection to military
development or possess features that may be useful in
military service. The question is whether that
connection identifies a historically recognized
boundary of the right, or instead merely describes a
modern firearm in terms that cannot substitute for a
demonstrated analogue. The Court must therefore
determine what Heller’s reference to M -16 rifles
actually establishes and whether it supplies the
historical principle respondents need.
B. Heller and Caetano reject military utility as
the test of protection.
The principal doctrinal objection to Amicus’s
position is Heller’s observation that the Second
Amendment does not protect an unlimited set of
weapons and that “M -16 rifles and the like” may be
banned. 554 U.S. at 627. That language does not
establish that any firearm with military lineage,
military-style features, or s ubstantial defensive
effectiveness is categorically outside the Amendment.
Caetano v. Massachusetts , 577 U.S. 411 (2016),
confirms that military utility is not a threshold
condition of protection. The state court there
concluded that stun guns lay outside the Second
Amendment because they were not readily adaptable
to military use. This Court vacated th at judgment
because Heller rejected the proposition that only
weapons useful in warfare are protected.  Id. at 411 –
12.
The distinction is concrete. The Second Circuit
described the M-16 and M4 as selective -fire firearms
whose operator can choose semiautomatic or
automatic fire. Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rts. v. Lamont, 153
F.4th 213, 221 –22 (2d Cir. 2025). It separately

13
described AR -15-style rifles as semiautomatic and
recognized that their primary difference from the M -
16 is the lack of fully automatic firing capability.  Id.
at 244 –45. An automatic weapon continues firing
while the trigger remains depressed; a semiautomatic
firearm fires one round for each trigger pull. See
Staples v. United States , 511 U.S. 600, 602 n.1, 603
(1994).
That mechanical distinction alone does not decide
these cases. But it shows why Heller’s reference to M-
16 rifles cannot be converted, without the historical
showing Bruen requires, into a general military -
association exception. A court may not substitute
labels such as “military-style,” “combat-functional,” or
“especially effective” for analysis of the historical
principle asserted. If the government maintains that
a class  of arms may be prohibited because of a
particular combination of firing capacity, destructive
capacity, dangerousness, or historical use, it must
demonstrate the relevantly similar historical
tradition.
This proposition has a defined limit. It does not
deny the government’s authority to regulate arms on
the basis of  a demonstrated historical tradition.
Common lawful possession is not the only
consideration, but it is constitutionally significant: an
arm cannot be treated as unusual while disregarding
evidence that law -abiding citizens widely possess it
for lawful pur poses. The argument instead rejects a
shortcut: the proposition that an arm otherwise
within the Amendment’s text may be excluded merely
by associating it with modern military equipment.

14
C. “Dangerous and unusual” is a historical
limitation, not a generalized dangerousness
test.
Petitioners’ position is not that “dangerous and
unusual” arms can never be regulated. It is that the
phrase is a historically defined, conjunctive
limitation, not a generalized dangerousness test.
Firearms are dangerous if improperly used. That
ordinary fact cannot distinguish protected arms from
unprotected ones, or the exception would swallow the
rule. The government must instead show that the
particular arm is unusual in lawful society and that
its categorical prohibition accords with a well -
established historical tradition. Military lineage,
claimed lethality, and legislative characterizations
such as “military -style” cannot substitute for that
showing.
Heller juxtaposed arms “in common use” with the
historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of
“dangerous and unusual weapons.” 554 U.S. at 627.
Bruen likewise explained that, even if handguns were
historically regarded as dangerous and unusual, that
history could not justify modern restrictions on
handguns unquestionably in common use today. 597
U.S. at 47. Common lawful possession is not the only
consideration, but it is constitutionally significant. A
court cannot characterize an arm as unusual while
disregarding evidence that law -abiding citizens
widely possess it for lawful purposes.
The relevant inquiry is therefore not whether a
semiautomatic rifle can cause grave harm if
wrongfully used —a premise true of firearms
generally—but whether respondents have carried
their burden to show a historical tradition of
categorically prohibiting a  class of arms that law -
abiding citizens possess for lawful purposes. The

15
government may not use present -day assessments of
danger, lethality, or military resemblance to create
the historical limitation it must prove.
D. The lower courts’ approaches depend on
variants of that unsupported proposition.
The lower courts use military resemblance as a
reason to exclude an otherwise bearable arm from the
Second Amendment. But the militia history on which
they rely establishes the opposite starting point:
citizens privately possessed the lawful arms that
formed the pool from which militia arms were drawn.
The lower courts thus invert the Miller–Heller
relationship between private possession and collective
defense.
The Seventh Circuit’s approach is explicit. In Bevis
v. City of Naperville , the court concluded at the first
step of the Bruen inquiry that the covered rifles were
not protected because they were much more like
machineguns and military -grade weapons than
firearms used for individual self -defense. 85 F.4th
1175, 1194–97 (7th Cir. 2023). In the decision under
review, Viramontes v. Cook County , the court held
that petitioners had not developed a record sufficient
to depart from Bevis. No. 24-1437, 2025 WL 1553896,
at *1–2 (7th Cir. June 2, 2025).
The Second Circuit reached the same terrain by a
different route. It assumed that the rifles were
bearable arms presumptively covered by the Second
Amendment, but held that Connecticut had
demonstrated a tradition of regulating unusually
dangerous weapons. Lamont, 153 F.4th at 233–55. In
applying that formulation, the court emphasized the
rifle’s military development, near -equivalent muzzle
velocity to the M -16, asserted combat -functional
features, and evidence concerning the comparative
effects of rapid semiautom atic fire. Id. at 242 –55. It

16
analogized the modern restrictions to historical rules
governing Bowie knives, dirks, and later machineguns
and submachine guns. Id.
The Seventh Circuit’s later decision in Barnett v.
Raoul underscores the issue and must be
acknowledged. After a developed record and a bench
trial, Barnett upheld Illinois’s Act as applied to AR -
15s and thirty -round rifle magazines. Nos. 24 -3060,
24-3061, 24-3062 & 24-3063, slip op. at 1 –2 (7th Cir.
July 9, 2026). Barnett concluded that the Act accords
with principles purportedly underlying a national
tradition of firearm regulation, including a tradition
of reserving especially dangerous weapons to military
use. Id. at 1–2, 10–12.
The contrary approach of the Third Circuit further
illustrates the question presented. In Ass’n of N.J.
Rifle & Pistol Clubs, Inc. v. Att’y Gen. N.J. , 183 F.4th
211 (3d Cir. 2026), the court held that New Jersey’s
prohibition on semiautomatic rifles violated the
Second Amendment. It concluded that semiautomatic
rifles are bearable arms within the Amendment’s text
and that the State had not carried its burden to show
a historical tradition supporting a de facto prohibition
on a class of arms in common lawful use. The court
further concluded that a history of regulating armed
threats or weapon misuse does not establish a
comparably justified tradition of generally prohibiting
possession of an entire class of firearms.
Amicus does not ignore Barnett’s record -based
treatment of the differences between civilian AR -15s
and M-16s. Nor does it contend that those arms are
identical. The issue is instead whether the
characteristics on which Barnett, Bevis, and Lamont
rely establish a historically recognized constitutional
category. Firing rate, muzzle velocity, ergonomic
features, military ancestry, asserted ease of

17
conversion, or comparative effectiveness may bear on
factual or policy judgments. But those features do not
themselves identify the historical “how” and “why” of
a categorical arm prohibition. Unless a demonstrated
historical tradition treats a relevantly similar class of
civilian arms as outside the right, those
characteristics cannot perform the historical work
required by Bruen.
A historical rule directed to threatening conduct
speaks to conduct. A restriction activated by a judicial
finding of dangerousness speaks to persons. A rule
targeting automatic weapons may speak to that
weapon category. And a status -based disability
speaks to the legal status of those subjected to it. None
establishes, without further historical support, a
general principle that a semiautomatic rifle becomes
unprotected because it has military associations or is
particularly effective.
E. The historical burden should be stated
precisely.
The question is not whether civilian possession
must mirror the equipment of a modern armed force.
It is whether the historical tradition recognized a
categorical rule under which an arm otherwise within
the people’s possession became unprotected simply
because it was effective for organized defense or
shared characteristics valued in military service.
The history developed above supplies no such
background presumption. It instead requires the
government to identify a genuinely comparable
historical principle. Petitioners separately address
textual coverage, common use, dangerousness, and
the historical analogues offered for these bans.
Amicus does not ask the Court to decide those issues
through a mechanical comparison of eighteenth -
century and modern rifle designs. Its contribution is

18
narrower: if respondents contend that military
association or asserted effectiveness itself places a
semiautomatic rifle on the government’s side of an
implied civilian-military line, Bruen requires them to
demonstrate that claimed arm -category principle in
the Nation’s historical tradition rather than assume it
at the threshold.
CONCLUSION
English law constrained prerogative disarmament.
The Founding paired federal military authority with
a right retained by the people and a militia drawn
from an armed citizenry. Reconstruction -era status -
based restrictions do not establish a tradition of
prohibiting classes of arms.
The history  does not establish a right to every
military weapon; it shows that military utility and
civilian possession were not opposing constitutional
categories. Because the lower courts identified no
historical principle under which military lineage,
military-style features, asserted effectiveness, or
generalized dangerousness removes a widely
possessed semiautomatic rifle from the Second
Amendment, the judgments should be reversed.
